notes.title: Scrolling labor
notes.body: 翻 is turning things over or paging through them; 全网搜索 later places this search online. 半天 often exaggerates a long while, rather than clocking half a day. The opening makes browsing feel like labor before a purchase has even happened. The sleepless nights then push that tiny inconvenience into a comic endurance test.

notes.title: Price taste

phrase.en: The ones I like cost too much

notes.body: The next line reverses the equation: affordable things are ugly. Both clauses omit the noun—“the ones I like,” “the cheap ones”—so the choices seem to sort themselves automatically into two unusable piles. The parallel phrasing does the work of the joke: more searching offers more options without producing a possible decision.

notes.title: Counterfeit
notes.body: The anxiety is not only whether he can afford something. It is whether the thing will be genuine and whether his taste will survive the purchase. That makes 假, “fake,” an early, literal version of a much wider album concern: recognizing sincerity, imitation and performance. Here those questions begin with clothes and the risk of wasting money.

notes.title: Heart cools
notes.body: 心凉 literally makes the heart go cold. The fear is of excitement collapsing once the purchase is made, not merely of receiving an unsuitable size. It sits neatly between a possible counterfeit and an offended wallet: the imagined loss is emotional, material and almost interpersonal at once. English “disappointed” conveys the result but loses that sudden change of temperature.

notes.title: The wallet becomes the offended party
notes.body: 记恨 is to nurse a grudge. His wallet becomes a wronged companion that can punish him for a bad purchase, even rejecting future 财运—financial luck. 拒收 is the practical word for refusing delivery, so fortune arrives like another online order. Nobody else has to criticize his spending: even the thing holding his money can judge him. The shopping vocabulary keeps running after the ordinary purchase has turned into a fantasy.

phrase.en: My wallet will hold it against me

notes.title: Tired refrain

phrase.en: Tired tired tired tired tired tired

notes.body: After all the comparing and second-guessing, the language reduces to one syllable, lèi, over and over. Nothing new needs to happen for the shopper to be exhausted. This short breakdown also makes the subsequent luxury of being “too carefree” sound suspect: the song has just let us hear how much effort apparent ease can hide.

notes.title: A tumble after success
notes.body: 翻跟头 literally describes a somersault; here it means a humiliating reversal. Listen to the three 太, “too,” statements around it: too carefree, too pleased, too smooth. Normally desirable conditions become warning signs. The verse keeps inventing a penalty for doing well, which makes the later command to go all in sound pressured as much as triumphant.

notes.title: Display
notes.body: 示众 is putting somebody on display before a crowd, often to shame or punish them. A 花车 is a decorated parade float, usually a vehicle for celebration. Combining them turns a festive public appearance into humiliation. That uneasy mixture prepares the emperor reference without requiring the listener to know the fairy tale in advance.

notes.title: Shopping anxiety becomes public exposure
notes.body: Andersen’s emperor walks through a public procession in clothes that do not exist, while the crowd pretends to admire them. This song has already imagined being stripped and tied to a parade float. The reference completes a nasty reversal: the shopper who cannot find the right clothes ends up unable to conceal himself at all. Taste and appearance become public vulnerability.

sources.label: Hans Christian Andersen Centre: The Emperor’s New Clothes

notes.title: Balloon
notes.body: Success becomes a balloon that can be punctured by bad luck. The image links height with fragility: rising is precisely what creates the possibility of a fall. Across these lines, the body tumbles, the crowd looks, and the balloon bursts. The eventual insistence on moving forward is made out of these feared reversals.

notes.title: The idiom behind “All In”
notes.body: 一不做，二不休 means doing nothing or, once committed, going through with it completely. It is stronger and more stubborn than ordinary encouragement to try your best. Its balanced one/two structure is easy to chant, and repeating it four times gives the speaker a ready-made answer to every preceding hesitation. The title “All In” catches that deliberate refusal of a middle option.

phrase.en: Once I start, I'm going all the way

notes.title: One cut through the mess
notes.body: 快刀斩乱麻 pictures a sharp blade cutting through tangled hemp: solve a messy problem decisively. The previous 坐以待毙 means sitting and waiting for death. These weighty set phrases arrive after a struggle to buy pants. Their disproportion is funny, but the sequence also shows how quickly a minor choice can acquire the emotional stakes of survival.

phrase.en: cut through the tangle with one swift stroke

notes.title: The shopping trip changes scale

phrase.en: Can't go home till I've made it big

notes.body: 做大 means growing an undertaking or career into something substantial; 回家 is simply going home. Repeated together, they turn home from a place of rest into a reward withheld until success. The shopping problem has disappeared, but its inability to settle has expanded. The ending keeps walking because the condition for stopping is never declared met.

tracks.intro: A search for the right pants spirals into fear of exposure, then hardens into an order to succeed at any cost.

notes.title: Test reward
notes.body: 测试 and 通过 are the terms of testing and passing; 奖励 supplies a reward. Together they make affection sound like an assessment administered by the other person. The politeness of 请问, “may I ask,” almost makes him a candidate asking when results will be announced. Intimacy begins under an unequal arrangement: one person evaluates while the other waits.

notes.title: Time ownership
notes.body: 最佳 is the optimum or best possible moment, stronger than merely “a time.” The other person can always defer commitment until conditions improve; he later answers that he is running out of time. The two voices of this imagined conversation occupy different clocks. One has the freedom to deliberate, while the other experiences deliberation as an emergency.

notes.title: Bad luck that sticks
notes.body: 霉运 means bad luck, while the character 霉 also means mold: the odd English title preserves that second meaning. The hoped-for “prize” appears earlier as the reward for passing a test of love. Put together, the title makes the entire reward system feel spoiled. 甩不干净 adds a physical detail: this luck sticks to him no matter how hard he shakes it off.

notes.title: The same overturned tracks
notes.body: 重蹈覆辙 pictures taking the same road on which a cart already overturned: failing to learn from a previous mistake. The next line, “Then let’s do it all again,” knowingly accepts that failure. Repeating the chorus makes the form enact the idiom. The speaker can recognize the pattern perfectly and still choose another pass through it.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 重蹈覆轍

notes.title: Playing house
notes.body: 过家家 is children’s make-believe domestic life: playing at being a family. Calling the relationship something more serious does not end its game vocabulary. The song soon calls it a cruel 游戏, and User116 describes gambling. The complaint is not that there are no rules; it is that one person keeps staking real feelings on rules the other will not make clear.

notes.title: Hearing
notes.body: The repeated question shifts the demand from being loved to being acknowledged. The first chorus asked whether feelings could pass a test; now the speaker cannot even establish that his words have landed. As the line returns, it works less like a request for new information and more like knocking on a door that stays closed.

notes.title: Simple question
notes.body: The lyric calls it a simple question, then spends several lines failing to obtain an answer. That mismatch is its frustration: “Do you like me?” can be grammatically simple while carrying consequences that make it difficult to say. The waiting person treats clarity as something owed, which gives the plea an edge of accusation.

notes.title: Gambling
notes.body: User116 changes the metaphor from a test into a gamble. Tests promise that effort can lead to a correct outcome; gambling admits that sincerity cannot control the result. 再, “again,” makes this a depleted return, and the next lines remove both the capacity to lose and the stake itself. The guest verse deepens the chorus by changing its model of hope.

notes.title: Bottled tears

phrase.en: No matter how I try, I can't hold it in.

notes.body: The pattern 怎么……都…… means the result holds however hard or in whatever way he tries. Repeating 憋 makes the failed effort audible: holding it in, then being unable to hold it in. The wording shares the physical pressure of “Numb,” where unspoken feelings are bottled up. Here that pressure finally reaches tears.

notes.title: Person heart

phrase.en: have you—I want your heart too

notes.body: 人 here is the person as a bodily presence or partner; 心 is their inward affection. The contrast asks for emotional reciprocity beyond merely being together. It also exposes how possessive the language of “getting” someone can sound: he wants certainty over something that cannot be delivered like the reward promised in the opening.

notes.title: Earrings
notes.body: After the abstract language of feelings, tests and final answers, the verse ends with a small piece of unworn jewelry. It is concrete evidence the speaker can keep returning to, even though it cannot settle what the other person feels. The gift has become a question: if the relationship matters, why is its visible token absent?

tracks.intro: Romance becomes a test with no results, then a bet neither voice can afford to lose.

notes.title: An afternoon off, enlarged into retirement
notes.body: 退休 normally means retirement from working life, yet the imagined reward here is only an afternoon alone with milk tea. That disproportion makes the wish both funny and affecting: he asks for an exit from the whole system to obtain a very small amount of unclaimed time. The song repeats the fantasy instead of specifying a career plan.

notes.title: Milk tea
notes.body: There is no grand scene of escape: just the everyday act of buying a sweet drink and being allowed to enjoy it alone. 独自享受 makes solitude a pleasure rather than a punishment. That small wish cuts through the tape’s recurring larger demands to make it big, earn money, be seen and keep going.

notes.title: Wilted flowers
notes.body: 鲜花 names fresh flowers, immediately contradicted by 早就, “long since,” and 枯萎, “withered.” What sounds beautiful has already used up its life. The image lets the song move from a mildly comic retirement wish into a sense that the period for thriving has somehow been missed. No explanation of the loss follows.

notes.title: Missing children
notes.body: The first-person fatigue suddenly opens onto an unspecified plural: children who have gone missing and have nowhere clear to go. The following narrow road sustains that disorientation. The lyric offers no incident or place to identify; its force comes from replacing the solitary adult seeking rest with people who cannot find a route at all.

notes.title: A crowded route
notes.body: 挤破头 means struggling so fiercely to squeeze into something that heads get battered. The narrow road makes opportunity spatial: even continuing forward requires competing for room. After the withered flowers and missing children, the familiar idiom becomes unusually physical. The exhaustion has a visible cause—too many people trying to fit where there is not enough space.

notes.title: A thankless effort
notes.body: 吃力不讨好 means working hard without earning appreciation or a favorable response. 吃力 contributes the strain, 讨好 the attempt to please. It follows the pair 费心 and 费力, spending mental attention and bodily effort. The accumulating phrases distinguish being tired from refusing a bargain in which neither kind of effort seems to come back to you.

phrase.en: All that work, and no appreciation

notes.title: The Korean refrain
notes.body: 오냐 is an affirmative response used to somebody younger or lower in status: closer to a familiar “all right” than a polite, neutral yes. Its repeated use gives Effie a rhythmically assertive entrance. The switch from Mandarin into Korean and then English marks a distinct voice taking over the song, with its own way of addressing the listener.

notes.title: Plankton
notes.body: Plankton shrinks the self to something tiny and carried by surrounding currents. Effie moves almost immediately from that image into trouble-seeking, style and self-assertion. The boast does not neatly cancel the smallness; the verse keeps changing scale. That makes her response to Jackzebra’s fatigue active and restless without making it simply more optimistic.

notes.title: Givenchy
notes.body: Givenchy is the French fashion house; the line is a compressed outfit detail. It arrives between lying on a dirty street and insisting that nobody will ruin her work. Designer clothing does not clear away the verse’s smallness or disorder. It becomes one of the things she can still assert about herself while declaring independence from the industry.

notes.title: Dance chaos
notes.original: dance while i’m singing in the chaos

phrase.zh: dance while i’m singing in the chaos
phrase.en: dance while i’m singing in the chaos

notes.body: Jackzebra imagines stopping work and sitting alone; Effie tells the body to keep moving while disorder continues. The connective word is “while”: dancing does not have to wait for a calm or repaired life. This gives the feature a distinct answer to the same exhaustion, and the return of his retirement refrain leaves both answers in play.

notes.title: G-DRAGON
notes.body: G-DRAGON is the Korean rapper and BIGBANG member. Naming somebody she misses interrupts Effie’s self-sufficient pose with fandom. The later “crayon” also sits beside a G-DRAGON title: his official tour release lists “Crayon.” That gives the drawing image a possible musical echo, while its immediate scene stays small and handmade, far from the industry she has just dismissed.

tracks.intro: The retirement plan is one quiet afternoon; Effie answers it with a restless, defiant voice from Seoul.

notes.title: Matching sneakers
notes.body: To cop something is to get or buy it; kicks are sneakers. The matching pair makes the purchase a sign of friendship before the verse begins distancing itself from the larger scene. It introduces the distinction that matters throughout: privacy does not mean having nobody. He can keep his circle small and still make belonging visible through a shared object.

notes.title: Staying out of the mix
notes.body: Staying out of the mix means avoiding the surrounding social drama or entanglements. The verse develops it through not talking, leaving after the show and blocking people while away. These are active boundaries, not simple shyness. By the last line, keeping “my people close” names the positive side of the same choice.

notes.title: D&G and Kiko
notes.original: D&G top and Kiko on the pants

phrase.zh: D&G top and Kiko on the pants
phrase.en: D&G top and Kiko on the pants

notes.body: D&G is Dolce & Gabbana; Kiko points to designer Kiko Kostadinov’s label. The abbreviated names assume an audience that can read an outfit from a couple of words. Their placement matters: these clothes appear on a performer who then collects his fee and leaves. Dressing recognizably does not oblige him to stay available to the scene.

sources.label: Dolce & Gabbana: company code of ethics

notes.title: Get paid, then leave
notes.body: Dip means leave. The clause compresses the show into a clean sequence: perform, get paid, disappear. It fits “stay out the mix” and the later admission that he misses his bed in Osaka. Travel and success are present, but the verse keeps valuing the ability to leave as highly as the privilege of arriving.

notes.title: Out of town for a photo
notes.original: OT new country just so we can take us a flick

phrase.zh: OT new country just so we can take us a flick
phrase.en: OT new country just so we can take us a flick

notes.body: OT is out of town; a flick is a photograph. Taking a picture together becomes an excuse for crossing into another country. The casual scale of that boast then meets its opposite in the Osaka line: international motion can be exciting and still leave him wanting his own bed. Those feelings do not need to cancel each other.

notes.title: Eli
notes.body: Eli points to Elipropperr, credited beside Kuru as the track’s producer. Naming the person in the room puts an actual working relationship inside a verse about keeping close to trusted people. The track credits let that reference stay concrete; the song does not need a generalized story about an entire scene to explain its small circle.

notes.title: The recruitment hierarchy
notes.original: I'm the first round pick, you not part of the draft

phrase.zh: I'm the first round pick, you not part of the draft
phrase.en: I'm the first round pick, you not part of the draft

notes.body: A first-round draft pick is chosen early by a sports team, marking him as a prized recruit. He contrasts that priority selection with a rival excluded from both the draft and the team. The sporting vocabulary claims competitive value and group membership at once: being wanted by the right people becomes a measure of rank.

notes.title: Imposter
notes.body: The mirror interrupts the sports boast: the first-round pick does not recognize himself. It is a compact change from how he ranks publicly to how he appears privately. Jackzebra’s later “Mirrors” performs almost the inverse, finding a flawless version of himself. One reflection reveals estrangement where the other supplies admiration.

notes.title: Fried
notes.body: Fried is slang for a mentally overloaded, exhausted or intoxicated state. The immediate consequence here is not processing what somebody said. “Unstuck” in the next line then supplies motion after that haze. The range of the word matters more than naming a substance: the verse moves from being unable to take things in toward doing what he can.

notes.title: Run it up
notes.body: With money as its object, run it up means increase the total. The surrounding instructions are practical and modestly worded: do his best, keep his cool, earn, keep close to his people. That everyday list sits under the earlier first-round-pick boast. The verse presents ambition as repeated maintenance as well as superiority.

notes.title: Refusal
notes.body: 拒绝 is refusal, here framed as something to learn rather than a natural talent. “Starting today” makes it a small declared change in practice. The line comes between insisting on being himself and taking in nourishment, so protecting an identity is expressed through an ordinary boundary: deciding what he will and will not accept.

notes.title: Chew it over
notes.body: 细嚼慢咽 literally means chewing thoroughly and swallowing slowly. 获取养分, taking in nourishment, makes the image about what he chooses to absorb. After learning to refuse, the point is selective intake: not every influence or demand deserves to get inside. A few lines later he becomes a dessert himself, turning from the person consuming to the person being chosen.

notes.title: No performance
notes.body: 一点……都不 strengthens a complete refusal; 演都不带演 is colloquial insistence that he will not even bother acting. The repeated 直接, “direct,” carries that stance into how he appears before the listener. It follows a verse by Kuru that mocks caring more about image than music, giving the two voices a shared suspicion of presentation for its own sake.

phrase.en: I'm not putting on an act at all

notes.title: Dessert
notes.body: The verse shifts from insisting on independence to making himself available as a pleasure in somebody else’s life. 你 can address a lover, a listener or both; the words do not force a choice. The food metaphor lets him offer sweetness without abandoning his distinctive “ingredients.” A guarded self becomes something you might willingly return to.

notes.title: Special ingredients
notes.body: 用料 usually describes the ingredients or materials that make a product. Calling his own ingredients special turns individuality into a recipe: the sweetness may be familiar, but its construction is his. The word 首选, first choice, then asks the listener to select him. This is vulnerability in the language of a confident product description.

notes.title: First choice

phrase.en: I hope I'm your first choice.

notes.body: He repeatedly grants the other person freedom to choose, then admits he wants to be chosen first. 希望, “hope,” softens what could otherwise sound like a sales pitch. The ending preserves the tension between being unapologetically himself and needing another person’s preference. Kuru’s competitive ranking has become a much more exposed request.

tracks.intro: Kuru keeps his circle close; Jackzebra turns guarded selfhood into a dessert he hopes someone will choose.

notes.title: Nothing left to take

phrase.en: Money? Got none—just one worthless life

notes.body: 要钱没有，要命一条 is a defiant formula: there is no money to hand over, only one life. Replacing the second demand with 烂命, “rotten life,” devalues even that last possession. Yoyi then says this supposedly worthless life is going extremely well. The opening is less surrender than a way of making himself impossible to threaten: what can you take from someone who mocks his own price?

notes.title: Two sets of behavior

phrase.en: One face to me, another behind my back

notes.body: 当面 and 背后 oppose being in front of somebody with being behind their back. 一套 names an entire way of behaving, not one isolated lie. The speaker claims to recognize both versions. It sets up the sarcastic politeness that follows: smiling, calling someone darling and inviting bigger promises can themselves become a second face.

notes.title: For good

phrase.en: You say it's for my own good.

notes.body: 为我好 is the familiar justification that advice or interference is being offered for somebody’s benefit. The response is only a smile. Once empty promises follow, that smile reads as recognition rather than agreement. Yoyi does not rebut each claim; he lets apparently caring language reveal its usefulness to the person speaking it.

notes.title: A pie made of promises
notes.body: 画饼 is drawing food instead of supplying it: an attractive promise that never becomes something usable. Its older form, 画饼充饥, means trying to satisfy hunger with a picture. Yoyi makes the metaphor literal by demanding a bigger pie because he is still hungry. The affectionate 宝子, “darling,” and dry 呵呵 laughter make the encouragement sarcastic. He exposes the offer without ending the performance, inviting the promiser to continue digging.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 畫餅充饑

phrase.en: Paint me a bigger pie, bigger still

notes.title: Mourn culture
notes.body: 缅怀 is elevated, commemorative language for remembering someone or something with feeling. Answering the question about dead culture with this word gives the complaint a mock funeral. It sits in a line crowded with English profanity and copycat accusations, so the dignified register lasts only a moment before the competitive banter resumes.

notes.title: A vulgar compliment
notes.body: 屌 begins as a vulgar anatomical word but also works as slang for formidable or impressively good. Here it is a style boast, strengthened by English “swag” and the refusal to be cloned. The following 烂命太好 turns the earlier “worthless life” inside out: the thing supposedly worth nothing is now enviably good. The humor depends on holding both claims.

notes.title: Giving face
notes.body: 给脸 offers somebody face—respect or a chance to retain dignity. Saying they reject it is a reprimand, not a generous offer still open for negotiation. User116 pairs it with an offer of money, so both material and social credit have been refused. The repeated 给……不要 construction makes the other person sound determined to waste every way of being treated well.

notes.title: Sleep routine
notes.body: User116 changes direction abruptly: the confrontation gives way to small instructions for getting through a day. Regular sleep, smiling and staying in the present are ordinary, almost rehearsed reassurances. The following admission that it will still hurt prevents the sequence from becoming effortless optimism. The verse wants improvement while allowing that repeated advice does not instantly deliver it.

notes.title: Money none

phrase.en: Money or no money, it doesn't matter.

notes.body: Repeating a noun around 不—钱不钱的—loosely dismisses the whole question of money. But the next line says what matters is using it properly, and soon he happily admits greed. The contradiction is conversational, not a formal economic position: money can be something he refuses to worship and something he still wants.

notes.title: Wechat rhyme

phrase.en: Fill my WeChat with good-looking people.

notes.body: 好吃的 and 好看的 use matching grammar: tasty things for the stomach, good-looking people for the contact list. The missing nouns let desire classify both as things he wants more of. He then chooses a good-looking feed background too. That small sequence turns taste, attraction and self-presentation into one parallel set of everyday appetites.

notes.title: Moments
notes.body: 朋友圈 literally means “circle of friends” and is WeChat’s Moments feed. A background image is part of how that small public self appears to contacts. Here it belongs beside food and attractive people as an ordinary pleasure. When Jackzebra later opens the same feed to announce universal death, the platform connects the verses: the location stays the same, but its mood collapses.

notes.title: Choosing ordinary appetites

phrase.en: worldly person—greedy for money, hungry for sex

notes.body: 俗人 places him among ordinary, worldly people rather than above material desire. 贪财好色 openly embraces two conventionally disapproved appetites, money and sex. After the routine of sleep, smiles and good food, the line refuses an elevated moral program. Wanting modest enjoyment and admitting unflattering desires become parts of the same decision to stay alive on human terms.

notes.title: An instinctive writing process

phrase.en: A song every half hour on average

notes.body: The production boast arrives after “let’s just mess around” and before recording whenever the mood takes him. It presents speed as a kind of freedom: making songs need not involve permission, ceremony or a grand statement. The computer and late-night voice give this philosophy an ordinary setting. The half-hour figure is the verse’s boast, not a stopwatch measurement.

notes.title: Calling his own singing a racket
notes.body: 鬼哭狼嚎 literally means ghosts crying and wolves howling, a set expression for awful wailing. Jackzebra applies it to his own recording immediately after calling music easy. That self-insult keeps the confidence comic. He gets to make noise on his own terms while anticipating exactly the complaint a tired neighbor might make about it.

notes.title: Reading out the names
notes.body: This phonetic roll call names the three credited performers: Yoyi, User116 and Jackzebra. 幺 is the spoken digit one, often used to distinguish it clearly when reading a number. Turning their names into 又一幺幺六杰泽比 makes the group sound like one continuous chant, briefly converting a set of separate verses into a shared signature.

notes.title: A feed-sized apocalypse
notes.original: 我微信222个人全部都死了

phrase.zh: 我微信222个人全部都死了
phrase.en: all 222 people on my WeChat are dead

notes.body: The oddly exact 222 makes the announcement sound like an inventory of actual contacts, then the claim swallows the announcer too. User116 has just filled WeChat with attractive people and valued staying alive; Jackzebra deletes the whole social world in words. It is an escalating performance of dismissal, staged on the very platform that keeps the people connected.

notes.title: Pronouns die
notes.body: The announcement moves through I, you, we and you-all before arriving at everybody. This is a deliberately exhaustive roll call, not just repetition of a punchline. Every grammatical place from which somebody could answer is folded into the joke. The final return to 命 then has a cleared stage: no particular person gets to escape it.

notes.title: Fate ending
notes.body: 命 has carried a life that can be offered up, judged worthless or enjoyed; here it becomes fate. English needs a new word, but Chinese lets the same syllable turn existence into a verdict. 不得不, “have no choice but to,” then insists on belief and acceptance. “Never Give Up” later reopens precisely this question by asking whether he must 认命.

tracks.intro: Yoyi turns low expectations into swagger, User116 chooses everyday pleasure, and Jackzebra sends the whole contact list into a comic void.

notes.title: Listen command
notes.body: The opening answers “what should I do?” with a small instruction to quiet the mind and listen. But the verse soon says not to speak, not to act and not to leave. The first directive can sound soothing until later commands reveal how easily guidance becomes restraint. The song keeps testing whether familiar advice makes room for him or closes it.

notes.title: Body
notes.body: An awkward, unglamorous bodily detail interrupts the instruction to become calm. Hair in the mouth and a body growing light do not add up to a named condition; they convey discomfort through sensations that are hard to organize. That matters beside the question of how to sort things out: the body presents the same problem as the crowded mind.

notes.title: Mysteries
notes.body: 未解之谜 is the sort of formal heading given to a puzzle that has not been explained. The verse applies it to unease picked up somewhere unfamiliar. It momentarily makes private discomfort sound like a documentary topic. A few lines later the documentary becomes explicit, linking the search for explanations to the making of a story about a life.

notes.title: Decide after the next step

phrase.en: take it one step at a time

notes.body: 走一步算一步 means deciding what to do at each step as events unfold, without a settled plan for what follows. English “one step at a time” can sound calmly methodical; the Chinese has more of “we’ll work it out as we go.” Next to unexplained sickness and mysteries, the line names an improvised survival method rather than confidence that the route is known.

notes.title: Microphone books
notes.body: 读书 can mean reading books or studying, so the line is broader than an inventory of leisure reading. The microphone marks a change in where knowledge comes from. The next sequence of inherited sayings complicates the joke: he can disclaim book-learning while demonstrating how much familiar cultural language is already lodged in ordinary speech.

notes.title: Bitterness and sweetness
notes.body: 忆苦思甜 means recalling hardship in order to appreciate a sweeter present. It also belongs to the vocabulary of Chinese moral and political education: institutions use the phrase for activities teaching gratitude through remembering difficult times. Here it joins a string of familiar maxims, yet the song supplies no convincingly sweet present. The next claim is that he already knows the routine.

sources.label: Ezhou Education Bureau: an 忆苦思甜 activity

phrase.en: Remember the bitterness, appreciate the sweetness

notes.title: Learning without the books

phrase.en: Live and learn, all your life

notes.body: 活到老学到老 literally keeps living and learning going until old age. It follows the claim that picking up a microphone ended his book-reading. The maxim can therefore sound both corrective and dryly comic: he may not be studying books, but experience is certainly continuing to teach him. The stock expression offers wisdom while the surrounding lines distrust stock routines.

notes.title: A familiar road
notes.body: 轻车熟路 pictures a light, easily handled vehicle on a familiar road. As an idiom it means being practiced and comfortable with a task. Put after “take it one step at a time,” it is a striking change in claimed competence. Before that confidence can settle, “you cannot run” turns the route into somewhere he may be forced to remain.

phrase.en: An easy ride down a familiar road

notes.title: You’ll be in for it
notes.body: 娃 is a child, but 你娃 can address a person directly in familiar or scolding regional speech. 遭, left without a full outcome, means they will come to harm or get what is coming to them. The warning is less polished than the adjacent four-character sayings. It sounds like somebody speaking close enough to threaten you in ordinary language.

notes.title: Retribution
notes.body: 报应 is the return of consequences for one’s actions, often understood as moral recompense. Here it follows prohibitions on speech and action, making restraint sound enforced by a punishment that need not be immediately visible. The sentence supplies certainty about the future precisely where the speaker’s own attempts to plan have been uncertain.

notes.title: Documentary
notes.body: The sudden film vocabulary pulls the preceding material into the frame of a work being made. The director’s early start is comically mundane after threats of retribution. It also places labor behind the image: somebody has to get up and organize this apparently unruly experience. The next untold jokes show that the material still exceeds the finished telling.

notes.title: Untold jokes

phrase.en: I thought of so many jokes,

notes.body: He has jokes ready but has not had time to tell them. Soon a sensitive child laughs to look strong. Laughter therefore appears twice as something whose outward presence can mislead: jokes remain unheard, while a heard laugh conceals pain. The song makes a distinction between having comic material and being able to use it freely.

notes.title: An unbothered exterior
notes.body: 大大咧咧 describes an apparently casual, rough-and-ready, unconcerned manner. It is paired here with a 敏感的娃, a sensitive kid, and then explicitly explained as acting strong. The outward laugh is not a contradiction to be solved: the lyric tells us it is the method of concealment. This is one of the tape’s clearest small portraits of performance as self-protection.

notes.title: Bound art
notes.body: 拳脚 means fists and feet and can evoke the ability to act or show one’s skills. Their restraint leads directly to the contrast between beautiful ideals and cruel reality. The phrase brings the complaint back into the body: artistic frustration is not only difficulty finding an idea, but being unable to put one’s capacities into motion.

notes.title: High artistic language, an ashtray ending
notes.body: 创作思想 is formal language for the ideas informing a creative work. The profanity punctures that high register, then the ashtray reduces the whole discussion to an object that holds spent residue. The ending is more pointed than “art is hard”: even the language used to dignify creation seems unable to save what it describes from becoming waste.

tracks.intro: Ready-made advice keeps arriving, but the speaker’s body, jokes and creative work refuse to fit its reassuring shapes.

notes.title: Oleander title

phrase.en: I can't make that mistake again.

notes.body: Asked in a June 2025 Interview questionnaire which movie he wished he could soundtrack, Jackzebra chose White Oleander. That supplies a useful connection to his stated tastes for the song’s title. Here the lyric stays with one-sided feeling, inability to speak and permission to leave; the film connection adds a point of entry without turning those lines into a plot summary.

sources.label: Interview: Jackzebra’s own listening and film picks

notes.title: Taking on, letting go
notes.body: 拿得起、放得下 praises being able to take something on and also put it down: commitment balanced by detachment. In this song the second half proves difficult. “Please don’t give up” follows almost immediately, so the maxim sounds like a posture the speaker is trying to acquire rather than a freedom he already possesses. Its repeated return does not resolve the attachment.

phrase.en: If I can take it on, I can let it go

notes.title: Still listen

phrase.en: I'll listen to what you say.

notes.body: The promise to listen offers cooperation without saying that the other person returns his feelings. In the next section, they do not even know about the attachment. That delayed information changes the opening plea: it may be part of an intimate conversation the speaker can imagine more completely than he can actually have.

notes.title: One sided
notes.body: 单方面 sounds like “on one side” or “unilateral,” comparatively dry wording beside 情, feeling or attachment. The phrase reduces an emotionally consuming situation to a simple imbalance. It also retroactively changes the repeated “don’t give up”: there may be no shared relationship for the other person to give up on in the first place.

notes.title: Unable speak
notes.body: The song can sing a plea repeatedly, yet inside its story the speaker cannot say the words. That is a useful distinction between a lyric and an actual conversation: the refrain gives form to what remains unspeakable in the scene. The empty head is not a lack of attachment; it is the point where attachment fails to become speech.

notes.title: Plain, calm, or dull
notes.body: 平淡 covers the ordinary, calm and unexciting; it need not mean an empty or failed life. Here it is given a 代价, a price: a blank head and words that will not come. That pairing makes uneventfulness costly without declaring that turmoil would be better. The speaker’s “I’m used to it” is then contrasted with somebody younger who may not be.

notes.title: Young
notes.body: 还, “still,” gives youth a time limit, while the next line says the other person will find this difficult to get used to. The speaker briefly assumes the voice of someone who has already endured what they have not. It can sound protective and resigned at once, especially when the promised benefit is permission to leave.

notes.title: Leave first
notes.body: 先 means first or ahead of somebody else. It keeps the image of two people on the same route even while allowing them to separate. Earlier the song asked the other person not to give up; its closing gesture removes blame if they do. That is a real change in what he offers, even if the feeling itself persists.

tracks.intro: The promise to let go keeps colliding with a plea to stay, until permission to leave becomes the only clear gift.

notes.title: Out before he can stop it
notes.body: 脱口而出 means words coming straight out of the mouth before they are weighed or restrained. The line follows “I feel it,” making expression seem immediate. Soon he decides that too much expression will look self-pitying. The miniature story is already in that reversal: what arrives naturally acquires an imagined audience and becomes something to regulate.

notes.title: An empty cooking pot
notes.body: 揭不开锅 literally describes being unable to open the cooking pot, an idiom for having no food to cook. Calling such worries “potential wealth” turns deprivation into something a writer might use. The reversal is uncomfortable as well as resourceful: creative value does not fill the pot now, and naming it wealth can make the original need easy to overlook.

notes.title: Saying too much
notes.body: 矫情 here means affected, excessively dramatic or self-pitying. It is a judgment about the presentation of feeling, not proof that the feeling is false. The speaker imagines looking this way to other people before he has even explained much. The word lets a social criticism become an internal editor, deciding how much pain he is allowed to say aloud.

notes.title: Happy miser
notes.body: 守财奴 is someone enslaved to guarding money—a miser, with 奴 carrying the word “slave.” Giving that figure happiness complicates the usual insult. He may possess what the speaker lacks, including the ease to judge somebody else’s worries. The line pits the earlier conversion of hardship into possible wealth against somebody already comfortably keeping hold of theirs.

notes.title: The tightening headband
notes.body: In Journey to the West, Tang Sanzang can recite a spell that tightens Sun Wukong’s headband and forces him to obey through pain. 念叨, nagging or repeatedly talking at someone, leads directly into that image here: another person’s repeated voice becomes physical pressure. The title “Curse” therefore names both a familiar literary device and the experience of carrying that voice around.

notes.title: Heavy head
notes.body: The literary headband first constricts; this short line makes it heavy. Later the weight moves to the shoulders as a 担子, a load or responsibility. The recurring pressure migrates over the body, giving different kinds of obligation the same physical effect. Two ordinary words briefly interrupt the more elaborate imagery to make that effect plain.

notes.title: The language of good company

phrase.en: Raise a glass and enjoy the talk

notes.body: 把酒言欢 is polished, literary language for sharing a drink and talking happily. It follows the blunt “short fuse” and precedes a request to finish the performance. Good company may therefore be a role maintained while irritation remains underneath. The sequence compresses a familiar social task: keep the occasion agreeable until it is safe to leave.

notes.title: Peach

phrase.en: Leave a peach too long and it goes soft.

notes.body: This homely observation arrives between maintaining a social performance and telling others to stay out of the relationship. Fruit changes when it is left too long; so do situations that are not addressed. The image adds time and fragility without spelling out a one-to-one metaphor. Its kitchen scale also recalls the pot and wealth at the song’s opening.

notes.title: Walking as a way through
notes.body: The song gives forward motion two different pressures: a heavy burden pushes him on, and the order never to look back blocks retreat. Walking is not simply optimistic progress in this setting. It is the narrow option left when stopping and returning both feel unavailable. That shades the tape’s repeated “keep going” language with compulsion.

notes.title: Clean hands
notes.body: The construction does not merely say the hands are dirty: washing fails to make them clean. That difference makes the stain feel persistent, something action cannot undo. The following refusal to turn back and confession to the air develop that persistence into a moral atmosphere. The song stays with the feeling of implication rather than specifying an act.

notes.title: Turning himself in to nobody

phrase.en: Confessing my guilt to the empty air

notes.body: 自首 is voluntarily turning oneself in, a word with an expected receiving authority. Confessing to empty air removes that listener, leaving the act suspended. The previous hands that will not wash clean give the gesture a sense of guilt without naming an offense. Speech happens, but it cannot obtain an answer, a judgment or release.

notes.title: Unwanted questions

phrase.en: Don't ask me so many questions.

notes.body: A song that began with feeling becoming speech ends by trying to stop a conversation. The questions themselves are something the speaker says he does not want to have. That folds curiosity back into pressure: being asked to explain can feel like another burden when he is still carrying the unresolved thing. The closing boundary does not supply a resolution.

tracks.intro: Private worries become usable material, but the voice judging them tightens around the speaker like Sun Wukong’s headband.

notes.title: A phonetic profanity
notes.body: This riffs on the established internet catchphrase 睡你麻痹起来嗨, “fuck sleeping, get up and party,” circulating in 2015 memes and music remixes. 麻痹 supplies a sound-alike profanity rather than a medical reference to numbness. Adding 给我, “for me / do as I say,” turns the invitation into an order. It is a loudly social opening for a verse about living in one’s own little world.

sources.label: Bilibili: 2015 remix of the get-up-and-party catchphrase

notes.title: Microphone sale
notes.body: The pants and microphone make a tiny checklist for going out into the street, and 开卖 announces the start of selling. Performance is presented with the casual practicality of setting up a stall. The shift from “get wild” to “get ready to sell” puts play and livelihood beside one another, without pausing to make them separate identities.

notes.title: Talking battles on paper
notes.body: 纸上谈兵 means discussing war on paper: theory or bravado without the practical ability to act. Jackzebra follows it with tantrums, an overloaded feed and diplomatic declarations. The idiom tells us what he thinks those actions lack—effective force outside words. Chun later picks up the same distinction by demanding confrontation beyond Moments and fan chats.

notes.title: Screen flood
notes.body: 刷屏 means filling a feed or screen with posts. It makes an outburst visible in volume even if it cannot make the person more powerful. The next lines supply official-sounding condemnation; later Chun mentions both Moments and fan groups. The song keeps distinguishing an audience for anger from an ability to act on it.

notes.title: A comments section speaks like a ministry
notes.body: 强烈谴责 and 严正抗议 are the official formulas “strongly condemn” and “solemnly protest,” familiar from diplomatic statements. Their placement after flooding a social feed inflates a personal quarrel to the scale of state affairs. Then “so what?” collapses the ceremony. The joke is in the register and its ineffective grandeur, not in identifying a particular diplomatic dispute.

sources.label: Ministry of Foreign Affairs: diplomatic formula in use

notes.title: Fooling ghosts
notes.body: 骗鬼呢 literally asks whether someone is trying to fool ghosts, dismissing a claim as unbelievable. The supernatural language becomes a bridge into the final verse, where people themselves are hard to distinguish from ghosts. What begins as a casual comeback grows into a picture of social relations in which appearances cannot be trusted.

phrase.en: Who do you think you're fooling

notes.title: The country-escape catchphrase

phrase.en: Too many scams in the city—I'm going back to the countryside

notes.body: Chun uses the familiar internet joke about escaping the city’s 套路, its elaborate tricks, by returning to the countryside. But his next line supplies potholes on the rural road. It denies an easy map with urban deception on one side and rural innocence on the other. The move changes the scenery without guaranteeing a less treacherous path.

sources.label: Xinhua report on the circulated phrase, via People’s Daily

notes.title: Holes and traps
notes.body: 坑 is both a hole in the ground and, colloquially, a trap, rip-off or bad deal. A muddy road makes the literal sense immediately visible; the preceding complaints about 套路 keep the social meaning active. The line is therefore a complete punchline in one image: even an escape from the city can land you in another kind of pit.

notes.title: A belly between you and a heart

phrase.en: You can't see inside people's hearts

notes.body: 人心隔肚皮 says people’s hearts are hidden behind the belly’s skin: outward familiarity cannot make their intentions transparent. Chun immediately attaches online aggression to that opacity. The verse does not ask whether the screen persona is authentic because screens are inherently false; it starts from the more ordinary difficulty of knowing what any other person really wants.

notes.title: The awkward bird gets an early start
notes.body: 笨鸟先飞 says the slower or less gifted bird should fly first—effort and an early start compensate for ability. Adding a body covered in shit ruins the proverb’s clean uplift. The bird may be working hard and still look filthy. A familiar lesson in self-improvement becomes an ungainly survivor, which fits the muddy road rather better than an inspirational success story.

notes.title: An old-fashioned address
notes.body: 娘子 is an older address for a woman or wife, giving the plea a theatrical, old-fashioned courtesy. It is surrounded by money, excrement and threats, so the register briefly changes character. The verse keeps desire for a kiss close to desire for success. Romantic address does not soften the whole speaker; it is another voice he can reach for.

notes.title: Money switch
notes.body: 跟我混 means hanging around with, following or making one’s way under somebody’s lead. One line earlier money has the speaker trapped; now he offers himself as a route to it. The switch is comically abrupt. The verse can recognize money as a constraint and still reproduce the recruiting boast that promises an escape through the right connection.

notes.title: A “teacher” of fate
notes.body: 老师 can respectfully address a skilled practitioner as well as a schoolteacher. Here the fortune-teller calls him, but later Chun insists that his progress came from no such master. 算命, calculating fate, is answered by 改命, changing it. The movement from receiving a prediction to claiming agency is one of the verse’s organizing contrasts.

notes.title: A film-star comparison
notes.body: Fan Bingbing is the Chinese screen star. “My Fan Bingbing” makes celebrity beauty a personal comparison inside the verse’s repeated call for a woman’s attention. It belongs to the same expressive jump as 娘子: ordinary desire is briefly enlarged into a dramatic, glamorous scene, before speed, smoke and confrontation take over again.

sources.label: San Sebastián Festival: Fan Bingbing biography

notes.title: Offscreen action
notes.original: 不是在朋友圈和粉丝群

phrase.zh: 不是在朋友圈和粉丝群
phrase.en: Not in Moments and fan chats

notes.body: Chun repeats Jackzebra’s distinction between talk and force but names the environments more precisely. 粉丝群 is a fan group chat, where an artist can rally an already sympathetic audience. Rejecting that arena questions how much courage it takes to perform confrontation among one’s own supporters. The claim is about where opposition happens as well as how loudly it is voiced.

notes.title: An aggressive “I”
notes.body: 老子 here is an aggressive first-person expression: the speaker magnifies himself through the authority of “your father / old man.” It is not the philosopher Laozi. The immediately surrounding regional phrasing gives the threat a direct spoken force that “I” alone would lose; English partly recovers that force through the profanity.

notes.title: Southern voice

phrase.en: So many people are ghosts; you can't tell them apart.

notes.body: The final guest is 南部犯罪份子, the artist Jackzebra named as his favorite SoundCloud rapper in a 2025 Interview questionnaire. This entrance changes the song’s scale: generalized tricks give way to friendship, parents, factory work and recruitment fraud. Attribution matters here. The feature adds a distinct voice whose distrust takes shape through a different set of ordinary social encounters.

sources.label: Interview: Jackzebra’s own listening and film picks

notes.title: Listen orders
notes.body: 听招呼 in this regional usage is obeying instructions or behaving as told, not merely hearing a greeting. The threatened consequence is confinement. It sharply revises Jackzebra’s earlier claim that nobody can control you: in this guest’s scene, authority may have somewhere quite physical to put an uncooperative person.

notes.title: Family and factory speech
notes.body: 老汉 is “Dad” in regional speech here, paired with the preceding mother. The parents 拼命, expend themselves to the utmost, to send the child out toward a future. The later factory labor and crooked broker put that hope into jeopardy. Keeping the family terms ordinary matters: the verse’s social stakes come from a household’s effort, not an abstract statement about migration.

notes.title: Cold heaven

phrase.en: Put on more clothes when it's cold; heaven wants you dead.

notes.body: The sentence begins with everyday care—wear something warmer—and turns instantly into a threat of annihilation. 天 does double work as weather in 天冷 and fate or heaven in 天要亡你. English has to change words to follow that turn. The same syllable moves from the world a parent helps you endure to a world that seems bent on destroying you.

notes.title: Factory brothers
notes.body: 打螺丝 is literally fastening screws and commonly stands for basic repetitive factory work. The ongoing 着 keeps the hands working while memory turns to friendship. This is a different image of the body from the excavator threats: it performs a small repeated task while the mind goes elsewhere. The following recruitment scam anchors that labor in a precarious route out of home.

sources.label: People’s Daily: a factory worker’s account of starting with 打螺丝

notes.title: Black broker
notes.body: 黑中介 is an illegitimate or unscrupulous intermediary. In this sequence—being sent out by parents, factory work, a rural newcomer—the relevant world is job placement. China’s labor ministry describes such brokers using false offers and inflated pay promises to take money from applicants. The lyric makes trust the point of entry: what is stolen first is the young man’s confidence in a connection.

sources.label: Ministry of Human Resources: recruitment traps

notes.title: A nail in the eye
notes.body: 眼中钉 is literally a nail in the eye: a person whose presence is intolerable and whom one wants removed. English “thorn in your side” carries the idiomatic meaning but changes the bodily violence. Coming after friendship mixed with interests and a cheated rural newcomer, the question asks how somebody can turn from a companion into an obstacle.

notes.title: Eating people

phrase.en: People who eat people become ghosts

notes.body: The verse’s ghosts are not safely separate monsters; exploitative people become them. After friendships mixed with interests and a fraudulent broker, “eating people” makes exploitation bodily and predatory. The repeated 鬼 has moved from Jackzebra’s sarcastic “fooling ghosts” to a social world in which a human face offers little assurance of human treatment.

notes.title: A knife made into a verb
notes.body: 刀, “knife,” becomes a verb: to knife or attack somebody. The repeated line switches from 他, “he,” to 我们, “we,” so the violent hothead is no longer kept at a comfortable distance. The ending implicates the speakers in the volatility they describe. That pronoun change matters as much as the threatening vocabulary.

tracks.intro: A party call turns into contempt for online posturing, then the guest verses bring that distrust onto roads, into factories and through the family home.

notes.title: Moonlight register

phrase.en: The moonlight is bright and clear

notes.body: 皎洁 is a literary adjective for pure, clear brightness, especially moonlight. It gives the opening a gentler and more polished register than the tape’s coarse insults and everyday commands. 隐约 in the next line makes the light faint on the face rather than dazzling: clarity belongs to the moon, while the intimate detail is only partly illuminated.

notes.title: Moonlight as a dress
notes.body: The grammar dresses the face itself in a wedding gown. Moonlight supplies the whiteness, so a passing visual effect creates the ceremonial image before any actual wedding is mentioned. That is why the next insistence on “our moment” works: the scene makes an ordinary shared night feel briefly set apart from the rest of life.

notes.title: Inner shout
notes.body: 呐喊 is a forceful shout or cry, but it is placed inside the heart. The question “can you hear it?” asks the other person to receive something that has not necessarily become outward speech. Against the quiet visual opening, that concealed loudness gives the scene intensity without breaking its intimacy.

notes.title: Present choice

phrase.en: I won't think about the future.

notes.body: The wedding image might invite thoughts of a shared future, but the speaker explicitly refuses to go there. He wants to treasure time at the scale of minutes and seconds. The tension makes the moment more particular than a generic promise of forever: closeness is valuable now, without its value depending on a guarantee about what follows.

notes.title: The landscape settles with him

phrase.en: The lake's surface will grow still

notes.body: The sequence moves from outside noise to the other person’s presence, then to still water and a changed mood. Instead of naming calm as an abstract emotion, it gives calm a surface that can stop moving. “Will grow still” also makes that relief something anticipated. The person need only be there for the world to seem capable of settling.

notes.title: Again courage

phrase.en: given me the courage to keep living again

notes.body: 又, “again,” suggests courage returning rather than being permanently secured. 活下去 emphasizes continuing to live onward. The gratitude is therefore substantial, but it stays tied to this renewed capacity in the moment. The sentence does not require the relationship to solve every other problem in order for its presence to matter.

notes.title: Two kinds of white
notes.body: 白白 means in vain or for nothing. Earlier 白 describes the white light and the imagined dress; doubling it now changes the meaning into wasted effort. The two meanings need different English words, so an audible link disappears in translation. That shift accompanies the verse’s move from the treasured present toward waiting for things that do not exist.

notes.title: Past private
notes.body: The closing description is bounded: 一场 makes it one experience, something with a particular span. Yet it can remain unforgettable even after the previous line allows the past to pass. The final claim that only two people know it preserves a shared private meaning without demanding that everyone else understand or validate the relationship.

tracks.intro: Moonlight makes an ordinary face ceremonial; the promise is to protect tonight’s closeness from noise, regret and speculation.

notes.title: Mouth edge
notes.body: 嘴边 places the words at the edge of the mouth, almost out. The following 说不出 means being unable to get them spoken. That spatial precision matters: the problem is not having nothing to say, but reaching the threshold and stopping. The repeated lines keep the listener at that same threshold with him.

notes.title: Pressure behind the numbness
notes.body: 憋 is keeping something in—breath, words, tears or emotion—under pressure. 默默 adds silence, 一个人 adds being alone, and 很久 adds duration. Those small modifiers make the repeated opening more than a generic inability to speak. In a song called “Numb,” the lyric is crowded with feeling that cannot find a usable exit.

notes.title: Shrinking his own complaint
notes.body: “Actually, it’s nothing” follows repeated descriptions of how much the unsaid words hurt. That placement makes it sound like the reflex of minimizing a problem after admitting it. The next line directs blame inward. The contradiction is recognizable conversational behavior: confession can be followed by an immediate attempt to withdraw the importance of what was confessed.

notes.title: Tied up inside
notes.body: 拧巴 is colloquial language for being twisted up, contrary or at odds with oneself. It keeps a tactile image of something that will not straighten out. The surrounding actions explain the knot: he cannot speak, cannot let go and still wants to try. “Tied up in knots” preserves that sense of conflict.

notes.title: Refuse release

phrase.en: still not willing to let those things go.

notes.body: 不愿意 is unwilling, not unable. After several lines about things he cannot do, the wording briefly assigns him agency over the attachment: part of him does not consent to its ending. That makes the knot more difficult than finding the right advice. Understanding that he might eventually think it through does not yet make him want to release it.

notes.title: Think through
notes.body: 想通 literally reaches a point where thought is open or passes through: arriving at an understanding that lets a problem settle. It contrasts with the twisted 拧巴 and blocked mouth. The lyric gives that opening to “sooner or later,” then returns to what he wants now. A future resolution is imaginable without being emotionally available in the present.

notes.title: Still salvageable
notes.body: 还有救 literally leaves open the possibility of rescue; in everyday speech it can mean “there’s hope for me yet.” 说不定, “maybe,” stops that hope from becoming certainty. The phrase follows a decision to try again before he has made sense of what happened. Action therefore briefly gets ahead of understanding rather than waiting for a complete explanation.

notes.title: The imagined alternative
notes.body: 另外一个世界 introduces an alternate setting where the speaker can be outstanding. The wishes that follow are strikingly conventional: youth, health, happiness and money. The extravagant thing is having them all at once with no remaining worries. The verse gives this complete package to an elsewhere, creating distance between the fantasy and the person still unable to speak here.

notes.title: Perfect list
notes.body: The short list of desirable conditions ends by declaring an entire life perfect. “Ah” gives the summary the flavor of a sigh or a small daydream rather than a practical plan. The gap between the compact, easily stated list and the difficulty of the opening is the point: it is simple to name an ideal life and much harder to inhabit one.

tracks.intro: The voice cannot release its words or its attachment, so it builds a perfect elsewhere out of very ordinary wishes.

notes.title: Beheading

phrase.en: every one of them should be beheaded

notes.body: 砍头 is an execution by cutting off the head. In a track that crowns its speaker emperor, it helps establish the theatrical role: he pronounces a collective sentence before arguing the case. The specificity makes the monarchy more than a generic rap rank. He performs the ruler’s supposed right to punish, then later sabotages his own exemption.

notes.title: Words and music
notes.body: 词 and 曲 split a song into its words and its musical composition. By naming both, the accusation claims that imitators want the entire construction rather than a stray phrase or surface style. That insistence on ownership prepares the joke at the end: the person defending every component of his originality eventually calls himself a thief too.

notes.title: Deluded hope
notes.body: 痴心妄想 dismisses a desire as foolish and unrealizable, more contemptuous than ordinary hopeful thinking. The little 有点, “a bit,” understates that rejection, making it sound casually devastating. This mock moderation is one of the song’s tools: he can order heads cut off, then act as if he is only offering a mild assessment of bad judgment.

notes.title: Bouncy insults
notes.body: 空空的, 麻麻的, 假假的, 瞎瞎的 and 丑丑的 give each insult the same doubled shape: empty, numb, fake, blind, ugly. Several also share the broad a vowel, helping the list fall into a taunting sing-song pattern. The childish simplicity is part of the insult. He reduces the rivals to a row of defective body parts and appearances rather than granting them an argument.

notes.title: Uneducated, uncultured
notes.body: 没有文化 commonly means lacking education, knowledge or cultivation. It does not mean having no cultural identity. Here the phrase is used as a mock excuse for swearing, immediately after a deliberately repetitive chain of insults. He adopts the judgment that might be made about his speech and turns it into permission to continue speaking that way.

notes.title: The emperor is made of the same stuff
notes.body: The soil metaphor briefly gives everybody the same material: “we,” including the speaker, are mud. That is a comic leveling inside a song devoted to ordering executions and climbing above kings. It also supplies a way to hear the final theft confession: no one in this patch of music is presented as existing completely outside its shared raw matter.

notes.title: Invite abuse

phrase.en: You can come curse me out now

notes.body: The speaker gives critics permission to begin, as though their reaction were another stage he has already scheduled. This is defensive control through anticipation: an insult loses some surprise when it arrives on cue. It also makes the “just playing” claim double-edged—he withdraws seriousness at the same moment he invites a contest over it.

notes.title: Serious joke
notes.body: 反正 means “anyway” or “whatever the case,” making the dismissal apply regardless of what the opponents say. It can protect the speaker from judgment while making a sincere grievance hard to deny: he has spent the opening claiming that others steal his work. The song keeps both investment and disavowal active instead of choosing one stable tone.

notes.title: His own earlier title
notes.body: 王中王 is the title of an earlier Jackzebra mixtape, so the boast refers back to a name already attached to his work. The line treats the catalog as a ladder of ranks: an existing king-of-kings title can be surpassed by a fresh emperor title. Its “last year / this year” contrast is the speaker’s promotional flourish, not a reliable dating guide for the whole tape.

notes.title: A bigger crown
notes.body: 王中王 is a king among kings; 皇上皇 places an emperor above emperors. Repeating the new name performs the promotion instead of waiting for anybody to grant it. The polite 请, “please,” makes the demand sound mock-courteous. The closing admission of theft then leaves the grand new ruler standing inside the same crowd he ordered beheaded.

notes.title: Royal names on the supermarket shelf
notes.body: Both royal names also belong to meat products: Shuanghui sells 王中王 sausage, while 皇上皇 is a Cantonese cured-meat brand. That everyday commercial layer makes the promotion funnier in Chinese. He can sound as if he is ascending above every ruler while also moving between names familiar from food packaging. The wordplay punctures grandeur without requiring the boast to stop.

sources.label: 皇上皇: official brand and product site

notes.title: Also thief
notes.body: 也, “also,” is the turn: the ending does not retract the existence of thieves but adds the speaker to them. The broad accusation at the start has become inclusive. It leaves several pressures visible at once—anger at copying, pleasure in a superior persona, and awareness that his own work also draws from things already in circulation.

notes.title: Stealing and sneaking

phrase.en: Steal, steal, steal, steal, steal, steal

notes.body: 偷 means steal; 偷偷 means secretly or stealthily. A long unbroken string of the character keeps both readings available on the page after the confession. The repeated syllable also abandons the earlier distinctions between lyrics and music for the bare act itself. English “steal, steal” catches the chant but loses the doubled word hiding inside it.

tracks.intro: A self-appointed emperor condemns imitators, crowns himself with names that also sell meat, then joins the thieves he began by denouncing.

notes.title: Warning
notes.body: 下场 is an outcome with a punitive shade: what becomes of somebody after an action. The opening connects it to not following another person’s instructions, then says the lesson has already been experienced. Before the ambition and self-confidence arrive, the song establishes a voice that remembers disobedience as something with a price.

notes.title: Bitter echo

phrase.en: The bitterness echoes on and on.

notes.body: Taste is described through duration and sound: bitterness reverberates. 苦 can already mean suffering as well as bitter flavor, so the line makes an unpleasant experience remain sensory after it is over. Its return before the new verse prevents the later efforts toward perfection from sounding untouched by what happened earlier.

notes.title: Headlong
notes.body: 横冲直撞 means barging about heedlessly, charging across and colliding. It rubs against the next ambition to be flawless: the method is rough while the desired result is immaculate. That friction makes the speaker’s self-description less straightforwardly heroic. Constant movement may express determination, but it is not evidence that the route is under control.

notes.title: Every move he knows
notes.body: 解数, pronounced xièshù in this expression, is a repertoire of moves or techniques; 浑身解数 puts the whole body’s resources into use. “Every trick” here is every available skill, not necessarily deception. The phrase adds bodily effort to the claim of trying different angles, just before that same body becomes unable to withstand attention.

notes.title: Nothing in one’s eyes
notes.body: 目中无人 literally places nobody else in one’s eyes: treating other people as beneath notice. A few lines later everyone’s gaze and the camera are fixed on him. That reversal changes who controls looking. The posture of ignoring others does not stop being exposed to them, and the bright attention soon becomes physically destructive.

notes.title: Quiet visible
notes.body: 宁静 and 孤独 share the same doubled 很 structure: very quiet, very alone. The next line abruptly adds being watched by everyone. Solitude and exposure therefore coexist rather than alternate. The song separates having attention from having company, which prepares the unreachable relief of the ice bucket.

notes.title: Bright light
notes.body: 打光 is setting or throwing light for a camera, a practical term from image-making. The next line turns that artificial light into sunlight heating the body. The shift is the hinge of the transformation: a professional condition of being seen becomes an elemental force, making the later snowman image feel earned by the sequence.

notes.title: Ice bucket
notes.original: 冰桶就在眼前我却够不到

phrase.zh: 冰桶就在眼前我却够不到
phrase.en: The ice bucket is right in front of me, but I can't reach it.

notes.body: Relief is not distant or invisible; it is right in front of him. 够不到 specifically makes it beyond the reach of the body. That is a sharper frustration than simply being overheated: the scene supplies a recognizable solution while withholding the ability to use it. The subsequent discovery that he is a snowman makes the urgency retroactive.

notes.title: Becoming a snowman
notes.body: The revelation is delayed: only after camera lights, heat and unreachable ice does he discover he is a snowman. Earlier details suddenly become parts of the same threat. Being illuminated, normally a sign of recognition, is precisely what this body cannot survive. The verse makes visibility and disappearance consequences of the same process, rather than opposite outcomes.

notes.title: Weightless

phrase.en: stop feeling the weight of my body

notes.body: Losing weight could have sounded like release from the tape’s many burdens, but here it marks physical disappearance. The snowman does not become freer; he loses the form by which he could be recognized. The line turns lightness into another danger, complicating the usual contrast between oppressive weight and welcome relief.

notes.title: The long river of history
notes.body: 历史长河 is the familiar “long river of history,” an expansive image for time and collective memory. His melted body enters it as an unrecognizable puddle. The grand scale does not preserve him; it dissolves his identity further. The next line states the fear plainly: the name and person may be lost even if some material trace remains.

notes.title: A bewildered morning
notes.body: 懵逼 is coarse, colloquial language for being completely stunned or confused. It breaks the elevated “river of history” register with an everyday, profane morning. “What the fuck” keeps that rupture in English. The phone then rings as if an ordinary day can resume, though the preceding scene has just made an ordinary, stable self difficult to take for granted.

notes.title: A new self for the morning

phrase.en: who I want to become today

notes.body: The final question is who he wants to become today, not what he wants to do. After the cameras and melting body, an everyday phone call treats identity as the item that needs choosing. It brings the surreal sequence back into a practical routine while leaving its central problem intact: being expected to appear before others as someone definite.

tracks.intro: Public attention becomes heat, the body becomes a snowman, and a morning phone call asks the vanished person to choose a new self.

notes.title: A little quiet
notes.body: 静一静 uses a repeated verb with 一 to make the action limited: settle down or have a little quiet. 一个人 specifies doing so alone. The request itself is small and temporary, even when sung insistently. The song begins by claiming enough space to hear oneself before it can arrive at any larger declaration of perseverance.

notes.title: Pronoun dialogue

phrase.en: How can you still not believe it?

notes.body: The opening “I” becomes “you” as the song starts asking questions. It can sound like self-address, an inner voice impatient with the person who keeps being surprised by the same world. The change lets the lyric stage disagreement without introducing another named character. The refrain then answers that questioning voice with an instruction rather than an explanation.

notes.title: Accepting one’s lot
notes.body: 认命 means accepting one’s lot, often with resignation. 难道 makes this a challenging rhetorical question, inviting a “no.” “Life Life Life” had insisted that fate must be accepted; here similar vocabulary creates an opening for 坚持, persevere. The song does not deny the cruelty it describes. It refuses the conclusion that recognizing a situation means consenting to stop.

notes.title: Perseverance repeat

phrase.en: Keep going, keep going to the end.

notes.body: 坚持 is holding on or persisting; 到底 adds carrying it through to the end. Repetition turns the advice into an action the song can perform: it keeps saying keep going. But no destination or reward is specified. The commitment is to continuation itself, contrasting with “All In,” where making it big is the explicit condition of going home.

notes.title: Still strength

phrase.en: At least I've still got the strength.

notes.body: 还好 is a small “fortunately / at least,” and 还有 means strength remains. The ending therefore scales the grand command down to what is actually available in the body. It does not claim unlimited resilience. The fortunate fact is simply that, this time, there is enough left to continue.

tracks.intro: A request for a little quiet becomes a conversation with the self, where accepting life’s cruelty need not mean accepting its terms.

notes.title: Courteous threat
notes.body: 请 supplies “please” to a warning surrounded by threats, so courtesy is doing coercive work. The later promise to stop being polite makes that tension explicit. The speaker presents himself as someone whose boundaries are reasonable and whose retaliation will be the other person’s responsibility. The civil phrasing is part of the threatening posture.

notes.title: Blade eye

phrase.en: A sharp blade leaves its sheath.

notes.body: 利刃出鞘 is a compact, dramatic image of a weapon being drawn. Its four-character form and the impossible speed that follows give the threat a staged, cinematic sharpness. The target is specifically the eyes, preparing a song preoccupied with looking and reflection. The next admission of being deep in a role keeps that performance frame in view.

notes.title: Bone and backbone
notes.body: 骨气, literally “bone spirit,” means backbone or integrity: the ability to stand one’s ground. “Spineless” preserves a comparable bodily image. The insult follows the spectacular threat to another person’s eyes, making moral weakness physically legible. It is the vocabulary of a speaker measuring worth through firmness, even while insisting that others must stop judging him.

notes.title: Choice
notes.body: 选择权 does not just mean a preference; it is the right or power to choose. The sentence makes sovereignty over the self the core claim beneath the insults. Yet the planned red carpet and arriving reporters show that this self still anticipates an audience. The song seeks control over the terms of attention rather than total disappearance.

notes.title: An unpleasant smell
notes.body: 腥味 is the raw, fishy or bloody smell of flesh. 人多 makes it increase with the number of people, so a crowd becomes a bodily substance before it becomes company. Generic “stench” conveys disgust but loses that fleshy specificity. The line supplies a sensory rationale for withdrawal within this particularly hostile persona.

notes.title: Deep in the role
notes.body: 入戏太深 means becoming too absorbed in a dramatic role. The next line insists he is never confused, so the speaker separates immersion from losing awareness. That distinction matters for the violence, mirror-admiration and red carpet that follow: he can perform the role intensely while also describing it as a role. The contradiction is visible within the lyric itself.

notes.title: Keeping oneself good
notes.body: 独善其身 can praise maintaining one’s own integrity, but it can also criticize looking after only oneself. Both meanings are documented in the dictionary. “Selfish and conceited” soon follows, preventing a purely virtuous reading. The compact phrase lets self-preservation and self-absorption touch: keeping oneself intact may also mean withdrawing concern from everybody else.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 獨善其身

notes.title: Holding the gaze
notes.body: 目不转睛 means fixing the gaze without turning the eyes away. Earlier the speaker imagined destroying another person’s eyes; here he cannot stop looking at his own reflection. The repeated eye imagery organizes the song’s power: outside looking is treated as intrusion, while his own looking supplies approval. “Flawless” arrives as a verdict from the gaze he permits.

notes.title: Mirror flawless
notes.body: 无瑕 means without a blemish. The mirror produces complete satisfaction here, but “Sweet” later turns a demon-revealing mirror on the self to expose its true nature. Those two uses offer a useful contrast: reflection can flatter or uncover. The album does not give every mirror scene the same reassuring function.

notes.title: Red carpet

phrase.en: The red carpet's been laid out.

notes.body: The scene moves from the private mirror to a prepared public entrance: carpet ready, reporters on the way. It makes the self-admiration part of a performance that is about to be seen. Hurry replaces contemplation. Even within the fantasy of complete control, somebody else’s arrival sets the timetable.

notes.title: Good person

phrase.en: I can't be a good person anymore.

notes.body: 不能再 frames goodness as a role that can no longer be sustained, and the next line supplies the reason: privately counted traps. The claim is more revealing than a simple boast of cruelty. It casts the hardened persona as something learned from injury, while the lyric still lets us hear how convenient that explanation can be for the speaker.

notes.title: How much is enough?
