notes.body: 胃口 means appetite and can extend to the scale of somebody’s demands. Saying it is small makes the request sound modest, but the next line still fears not having enough. That insecurity survives all the flawless reflection and red-carpet expectation. The body wants a guarantee the public image cannot provide.

notes.title: Denial ending

phrase.en: with cancer, but afraid to get treatment.

notes.body: The closing accusation pictures an extreme condition being left untreated while spending continues. It ends the contrast between the speaker’s fear of hunger and other people’s waste with an image of denial. The sharp turn from money to the body makes the accusation more than ordinary envy: resources are plentiful, but facing damage is continually deferred.

tracks.intro: A threatening, self-admiring persona guards the right to look at itself, while appetite and insecurity remain visible under the red-carpet confidence.

notes.title: Knowing exactly how far to go
notes.body: 分寸 is the appropriate degree, boundary or tact a situation requires; 拿捏 means handling it with control. Together they boast of calibrated judgment, more specific than ordinary “balance.” The next lines give that judgment muscle memory and the authority of a veteran craftsperson. Skill is represented as something already embodied, requiring no visible hesitation.

notes.title: A practiced hand
notes.body: 老师傅 respectfully names an experienced craftsperson or skilled worker. It conveys competence acquired through practice rather than the mystical authority English “master” can suggest. Beside muscle memory and chess moves, it gives the opening a whole vocabulary of accumulated expertise. The later inability to find the way home makes that mastery deliberately incomplete.

notes.title: Chess

phrase.en: I've already made every move on the board.

notes.body: 早已 makes the planning already complete, and 每一步 claims every step. The chessboard puts uncertainty under control before the song moves into wandering and not knowing where to fly. That contrast is productive: mastery over a sequence of moves does not automatically supply somewhere to belong. The song lets strategic competence and disorientation inhabit the same voice.

notes.title: Flight pressure

phrase.en: After the big rises and falls, my ears always ring.

notes.body: 大起大落 conventionally means dramatic changes of fortune. Thoughts “flying” in the previous line make those rises and falls physical, and ringing ears give the figurative altitude a bodily aftereffect. The listener can hear career or emotional fluctuation and feel pressure at the same time. The lyric extends an idiom instead of simply naming it.

notes.title: A place out of the wind
notes.body: 避风塘 is a sheltered basin where boats can escape wind and rough weather. Coming after thoughts in flight and years of 闯荡, making one’s way through the world, it offers a place to stop without making stopping a defeat. The question that follows is not whether shelter would be welcome, but where such a place can actually be found.

notes.title: Home control

phrase.en: I can't find the way home.

notes.body: The opening expert who has already made every chess move cannot solve the most ordinary navigation problem. That is the point of the reversal: being capable and confident does not guarantee a route back to safety. The next hoarse shout gives that lack a bodily cost, before he tries to answer it with yet more effort.

notes.title: A body that cannot be written off
notes.body: 报废 is declaring machinery, vehicles or equipment unusable and taking it out of service. Applied to the self, it turns exhaustion into the risk of becoming spent equipment. The reason given is that prior effort would otherwise be wasted. The lyric exposes a harsh condition for resting: even the worn-out body has to justify what has already been invested in it.

notes.title: Effort with a life at stake
notes.body: 拼命 means exerting everything one has, literally staking life in the effort. The conjunction 所以, “so,” makes it the consequence of not being understood: recognition must be pursued through even more work. “Sweet” later says there is no need to 拼命. The phrase connects two conflicting ways of answering the same pressure, without requiring the tape to settle on one.

notes.title: Freedom mission
notes.body: 任务 is a task or mission, and its importance is paired with a prohibition on mistakes. Soon the speaker praises a free, unrestrained life. The adjacency makes freedom demanding: he controls his own activity, but he also carries its deadlines and rules inside himself. Nobody else has to appear on the page to issue them.

notes.title: Firm tofu
notes.body: 老豆腐 is firm tofu, not old or spoiled tofu. Its whiteness develops 清白, a clean conscience, and its firmness supports the refusal to fall apart under boiling. There is also a familiar linguistic background: the saying about scallions mixed with tofu ends in 一清二白, punning clear innocence with green and white colors. Here everyday food becomes an unexpectedly durable portrait of integrity.

sources.label: Taishan College of Science and Technology: a tofu-making workshop

notes.title: His way of doing things
notes.body: 道 can be a road, a way of doing things or a guiding principle. The following challenge—how will you block it?—keeps the literal road alive inside the declaration. The line moves from having no route home to asserting a route of his own. That reversal makes the way both a direction of travel and a claim to live on his own terms.

notes.title: Throw fit
notes.body: 撒泼 means making an unruly, unreasonable scene to get one’s way. The speaker introduces it with 无奈之下, having no other option. That pairing presents loss of composure as a last available tactic. It undercuts the opening claim to perfectly measured judgment without erasing the conviction that he has a grievance worth pressing.

notes.title: An unsettled account
notes.body: 帐 is an account or ledger, and 没完 means it is not finished. A grievance becomes an unsettled balance still owed between two people. English “settling a score” uses a comparable transfer from accounting to conflict. The financial image also anticipates the later claim that others should have “bet” on him sooner: recognition and repayment keep borrowing the same vocabulary.

notes.title: A dangerous invitation
notes.body: At the Hongmen banquet in Sima Qian’s history, Fan Zeng arranges a sword dance as cover for killing Liu Bang during Xiang Yu’s feast. The name has become shorthand for hospitality hiding danger. The next lyric’s “acting skills” is especially apt: the historical threat was itself disguised as entertainment. Polite performance and hostile intention occupy the same room.

sources.label: Sima Qian: the Hongmen banquet in 項羽本紀

notes.title: Closed room
notes.body: 闲人勿扰 has the clipped tone of a sign on a door: people without business here should stay out. The next line shuts the room tight, while the speaker narrates what “they” are discussing inside. The sequence turns exclusion around. He may be outside their conversation, but the song lets him supply its embarrassing content.

notes.title: Betting on a person
notes.body: 押 is staking a bet. The imagined doubters do not merely regret failing to like him; they regret failing to back him while the outcome was uncertain. Their recognition arrives as a missed opportunity. The line turns exclusion into evidence of their poor judgment, letting the speaker narrate the private conversation he assumes they are now having.

notes.title: Recognition on whose terms?
notes.body: “Fresh” asks what is new; “classic” asks what deserves lasting recognition. The answer to both is the person already in front of the listener. The repeated questions make praise feel overdue rather than speculative. After so much movement, missed attention and private discussion, the song ends with a deliberately simple location: here, within sight.

tracks.intro: Expertise promises control, but the practiced body still gets lost; the voice answers with a firm block of tofu and a demand to be recognized now.

notes.title: Love of country as a ledger

phrase.en: Who dares say I don't love China

notes.body: 谁敢, “who dares,” makes the opening a challenge, not a quiet declaration of affection. The answer is an itemized account: taxes, spending foreign earnings at home, paying for a show and covering other people’s travel. Abstract belonging is made to face a ledger of actions. The repeated question lets the speaker demand judgment on those terms rather than accept somebody else’s test.

notes.title: Tax drugs

phrase.en: I pay my taxes, don't do drugs,

notes.body: Two ordinary claims of lawful behavior become the opening evidence in a defense of patriotism. The verb form 交着 makes tax payment ongoing. Later 本人, “I personally,” gives a declaration about legality the tone of a formal statement. The speaker alternates bureaucratic respectability with profanity, using each register to mock the conditions under which he is being judged.

notes.title: Economic register
notes.body: This is the formal language of a policy report, arriving after the practical act of spending money earned abroad. The enlarged description is funny because the individual purchase suddenly becomes a contribution to social development. It also makes the defense hard to brush off: the speaker borrows the elevated terms of evaluation and insists his ordinary actions qualify.

notes.title: Own pocket

phrase.en: Put up 20,000 of my own money

notes.body: 自掏 emphasizes money coming from his own pocket. 免费 makes the event free for the audience, not costless to produce. That difference is the substance of his claim: a public benefit can depend on a private expense people do not see. The round figure makes the contribution sound materially countable rather than merely virtuous.

notes.title: Flights and hotels
notes.body: 机酒 compresses 机票, plane tickets, and 酒店, hotels, into two characters. 报 is the practical language of covering or reimbursing an expense. The phrase makes the defense unusually concrete: support for other people has receipts, travel arrangements and a bill. It also briefly brings a working performer’s logistics into the grander rhetoric about loving a country.

notes.title: An unresolved target
notes.body: 根茎 literally means a root and stem, but 摸着, fondling, makes the bodily and sexual insult hard to miss. The opponent is pictured as deriving authority from intimacy with a “music uncle,” rather than producing an independent idea. What the line clearly supplies is a vulgar image of deference under the following mock praise for a great intellectual leader.

notes.title: Scolding the scolders
notes.body: 成何体统 is a formal rebuke about proper conduct, the language of an elder or authority demanding decorum. Jackzebra borrows that voice immediately after the mock title “great philosophical leader” and his own self-abasing “hip-hop moron.” The register change turns the accusation back on its supposed superior: if you are so elevated, why are you behaving like this?

notes.title: Thunder without rain
notes.body: 雷声大雨点小 means a lot of thunder with little rain: impressive noise followed by little result. The next image makes that noisy agitation into little monkeys jumping around. The idiom strips the antagonists of the power their activity claims, preparing the speaker’s casually cruel invitation to keep getting angry.

phrase.en: lots of thunder and hardly any rain

notes.title: Zoo gates
notes.body: After calling his antagonists monkeys, he says they have never left the zoo. The enclosure extends the animal insult into a claim about limited experience: loud judgment comes from inside a bounded world. Against his earlier movement between foreign earnings and domestic spending, the image makes range of experience another contested source of authority.

notes.title: A taunt disguised as encouragement

phrase.en: Make sure you try harder in your next life

notes.body: The grammar sounds encouraging—“make sure you work hard”—but the next chance has been postponed until another lifetime. That is the insult. It follows “die mad” and leads into the affectionate “little darlings,” so supportive phrasing is repeatedly used to belittle. The encouragement works by imposing a very long wait.

notes.title: Anger cutesy
notes.body: 宝贝们 is affectionate and plural, but 自卑 assigns the recipients insecurity. The phrase performs tenderness while claiming the authority to explain their anger for them. It belongs with “try harder next life”: the antagonism repeatedly arrives dressed as care. English needs the surrounding taunts to keep “darlings” from sounding genuinely consoling.

notes.title: Influence recast as missionary work
notes.body: 传教 literally means spreading a religion. Applied to the rivals’ cultural taste, it makes them followers of a doctrine handed down by somebody else. 糟粕 is the dregs or discarded residue, so even that received wisdom is downgraded. The accusation is sharper than ordinary copying: they claim authority while treating another person’s leftovers as revelation.

notes.title: His own complaint about overreading

phrase.en: reading a bit too much into it

notes.body: 想得有点多 is a conversational way of saying somebody is reading too much into things or imagining implications that are not there. 有点, “a bit,” gives the accusation a superficially mild form after several much harsher insults. The address still remains personal. The song resists being told what it must stand for by reducing the opponent’s theory to overthinking.

notes.title: Faces and hidden knives
notes.body: 两面三刀 is a fixed expression for duplicity—different faces in different company, with harm concealed beneath them. It works through an accumulation of surfaces and weapons rather than literally counting knives. Calling that figure a spy intensifies the mistrust: bad faith becomes the role of someone secretly serving another interest.

notes.title: A nationally charged insult
notes.body: 汉奸 is a charged accusation of betraying China or Chinese people for an outside interest. It is not interchangeable with an ordinary personal traitor. The comparison says even that figure is outdone by the opponent, escalating the national-loyalty rhetoric to absurd intensity. Jackzebra had already used 汉奸 as a song title on his earlier 王中王 mixtape.

sources.label: jackzebra: official discography, 王中王 track 34

notes.title: Inspiration conversion
notes.body: This is the title’s payoff: people and things that irritate him become usable creative material. The boast changes the outcome of the dispute. Even if the antagonists keep talking, their activity now feeds his songs. The later pocketing of creatures turns that conversion into a small collecting game, giving the voice a comic route out of indignation.

notes.title: A possible Pocket Monsters wink

phrase.en: stuff them all in my pocket

notes.body: The paired 精灵, little creatures, and 口袋, pocket, evoke Pokémon’s Pocket Monsters name and its Chinese “pocket creatures” associations. The word pairing gives the preceding insults a playful second scene. Each strange antagonist can be pocketed as another piece of material for a song: collecting irritations becomes a way to turn them into something useful.

notes.title: One ear
notes.original: 一只耳朵进一只耳朵出

phrase.zh: 一只耳朵进一只耳朵出
phrase.en: In one ear and out the other

notes.body: The same idiom works naturally in English: words pass through without being retained. Here it follows the accusation that someone cannot distinguish kind speech from abuse and leads into an instruction to read more. Hearing, interpreting and learning are separated into three failures. The demand for better judgment is expressed through a deliberately elementary lesson.

notes.title: The elevated family of China
notes.body: 华夏 is a literary-cultural name for China; 儿女 casts belonging as membership in one family. That elevated kinship language is immediately followed by calling someone stupid as a pig. The collision is the point. Solidarity does not magically erase the anger, and the final same-root poem must speak across insults the song itself is still delivering.

notes.title: Born from one root
notes.body: The ending quotes the Seven-Step Poem, traditionally attributed to Cao Zhi. Beans are boiled over a fire made from their own stems: beings from one root destroy one another. Following “children of China,” the image asks why shared belonging has become a reason to attack rather than protect. The grand historical quotation lands after deliberately childish taunts, making the closing appeal both pointed and uneasy.

phrase.en: We were born from the same root

tracks.intro: A defense of belonging turns taxes and travel receipts into a taunt, then converts antagonists into source material and ends on a plea against attacking one’s own.

notes.title: Right paths

phrase.en: Every path was the right one.

notes.body: 所有, every, leaves no wrong turn outside the opening verdict. Yet the song that follows is full of exhaustion, disappointment and self-questioning. The confidence therefore sounds retrospective: a route can have been worth taking without every moment on it having felt right. The closer begins with affirmation, then refuses to tidy up what that affirmation cost.

notes.title: Own eye
notes.body: 眼光 is judgment, discernment or taste as well as an eye’s reach. The self-congratulation plants the visual vocabulary that will become magnifying glass, telescope and mirror. At first he praises his ability to choose; later the useful vision is the ability to see himself. The track gradually turns outward-looking taste toward self-recognition.

notes.title: Taking notes on ordinary life
notes.body: 实习记者 is an intern or trainee reporter, a modest job title inside a song that later claims first place. The image makes music a place to observe and record before it is a place to rule. “Mirrors” anticipated reporters coming to inspect him; here he gives himself the reporter’s role. He moves from being looked at to finding words for what he sees.

notes.title: The same word for formulas and scams
notes.body: 套路 can be an established sequence, a formula or a manipulative routine. The next line’s repeated melodies brings the word directly into music, while “Ghost Dog” used it for distrusted social behavior. The recurrence connects two frustrations without making them identical: a predictable song and a predictable interaction can both feel as though the outcome has been arranged in advance.

notes.title: An easy ascent that still leaves wealth distant
notes.body: Immediately after rejecting shortcuts and reaching the summit in one step, the lyric puts people inside an elevator looking toward distant wealth. They have a mechanical route upward, yet the desired destination remains far away. The sigh punctures the fantasy of easy ascent. Movement and attainment are separated in a few ordinary objects.

notes.title: Wealth mountains
notes.body: Gold and silver become entire mountains, giving wealth a size that overwhelms the people inside the elevator. The preceding 登顶, reaching a summit, makes the mountains both treasure and destination. This is aspiration rendered as landscape: something visible in the distance can structure a life’s motion while remaining out of reach.

notes.title: A mirror that exposes monsters
notes.body: A 照妖镜 reveals the original form of a disguised demon; figuratively, it exposes what is genuine or false. He turns this revealing instrument toward himself. A magnifying glass examines closely, a telescope reaches far away, but neither substitutes for recognizing his own nature. That makes the mirror less flattering than the one in “Mirrors,” and more useful.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 照妖鏡

notes.title: Blessing
notes.body: 福气 names good fortune or the benefit of being blessed. The “real” version here is not first place or the gold-and-silver mountains: it is being able to recognize his own nature. “Mirrors” had good fortune shining beside a flawless reflection. The changed emphasis keeps the album’s language of blessing active while revising what counts as a fortunate outcome.

notes.title: Machine
notes.body: 台 is the classifier for a machine, and 一台 makes the whole world one piece of equipment. The next complaint is that being himself is difficult because so many things affect him. The image supplies pressure and interdependence without explaining a complete system. It lets the lyric register being acted on before turning to the private war he fights inside that world.

notes.title: Private war
notes.body: 自己的 locates the conflict with the speaker, even though the previous lines describe forces acting on him from outside. The battle is not given a named enemy or a decisive victory. Its consequence is ongoing wear on mind and soul, followed by the unsettling claim to love the pain. The verse asks what sustained struggle does to the person who makes it habitual.

notes.title: Time boils the rain
notes.body: 时间煮雨 is also the title of Yisa Yu’s 2013 song for the film Tiny Times. The exact phrase supplies a recognizable Mandopop echo here. Grammatically it makes time perform an impossible kitchen action, boiling rain, inside a reflection on two years of experience. The wording borrows an atmosphere of time passing without needing to reproduce or retell the other song.

sources.label: Yisa Yu: 时间煮雨, Tiny Times film song

notes.title: First place
notes.body: 这 makes first place something immediate and claimable, and 谦让 in the next line refuses the polite act of yielding it. This competitive certainty interrupts reflection on torment and wanting things to end. It prevents an easy reading of the closer as simple withdrawal. The wish to stop and the determination to win remain in the same voice.

notes.title: Rollercoaster

phrase.en: A roller coaster without an end

notes.body: A roller coaster promises controlled ups and downs followed by an exit. Removing the end leaves the sensation without the reassurance that it is temporary. The preceding pairs move from anticipation to loss, excitement to numbness; the ride turns those emotional changes into a track laid out in advance. Repetition becomes tiring even when the peaks are real.

notes.title: A life reduced to a swipe

phrase.en: One swipe of a thumb and it's gone

notes.body: The long emotional ride shrinks to a single movement of a thumb. The natural scene is scrolling: anticipation, work, excitement and disappointment can disappear from somebody else’s attention almost instantly. 一划而过 stresses passing straight over. The mismatch in duration gives the line its sting—the maker lives a cycle the viewer can traverse in one gesture.

notes.title: Playing after insisting on first place
notes.body: The instruction to keep it playful echoes a recurring concern in Jackzebra’s catalog: his 2024 弓长张 EP includes 认真你就输了, whose title says taking it seriously means losing. Here the advice clashes with the refusal to surrender first place just earlier. Play is both a creative freedom and a defense against how much the contest already matters.

notes.title: No self sacrifice

phrase.en: No need to give your life to it.

notes.body: 拼命 means exerting oneself to the utmost and literally stakes life in the effort. “Ume” had treated it as the unavoidable answer to not being understood; this line withdraws that necessity. The key word is 必要, necessary. The song does not have to abandon caring in order to ask whether total self-expenditure is really required.

notes.title: Immortal as a laughingstock
notes.body: 名垂青史 usually celebrates a name preserved in history. Adding 笑柄, a laughingstock, reverses the honor: lasting remembrance becomes lasting ridicule. This answers “Morning,” where dissolving into the river of history meant nobody would remember him. Across the two songs, being forgotten and being remembered wrongly become rival fears.

notes.title: Answering an older title
notes.body: This rewrites the title of Zhang Chu’s song 孤独的人是可耻的, “Lonely people are shameful.” Jackzebra inserts a forceful denial, then eventually replaces shame with greatness. The word 绝对, absolutely, stays fixed while the judgment changes. Repetition first defends lonely people from contempt, then claims positive value for them. The following muttering brings that grand declaration back to one person’s voice.

sources.label: Zhang Chu: 孤独的人是可耻的

notes.title: Talking to himself, then out of words
notes.body: 无语 commonly expresses exasperation, disbelief or having no adequate response, not literal loss of speech. It shares 语, “speech,” with the preceding 自语, talking to oneself. The paired words let him keep narrating while claiming to be beyond words. The song stages that contradiction rather than hiding it: speechlessness itself becomes another line to say.

notes.title: What recognition adds
notes.body: 期盼 is expectant hope, softer on its face than a demand. The following “invisible pressure” names what those hopes become for the person expected to fulfill them. No hostile audience is required for the burden to exist. The song makes a distinction between what listeners may wish generously and what the performer must carry inwardly.

notes.title: From knowing everything to trusting ignorance
notes.body: 无知是一种幸福 returns from near the beginning of “Anti Social Social Club,” bringing an earlier claim back almost as a remembered refuge in the final song. Near the start of “Sweet,” he said he knew everything going on. At the end, knowledge has become something to want relief from. Declaring absolute belief in ignorance leaves a pointed contradiction as the tape’s last thought.

notes.title: Belief ending
notes.body: 深信不疑 is a firm idiom for profound, unquestioning belief. Its object is the claim that ignorance brings happiness, so the song ends with certainty about the value of not knowing. After self-examination and awareness of treacherous hearts, that conviction sounds like a refuge constructed in language. The repeated affirmation does not erase everything he has just shown us he knows.

tracks.intro: The final track measures the cost of being seen, argues with its own competitive drive, and turns shame over solitude into a small act of defiance.
